paper_title: OSWAM: An Effective World Action Model with One-Step Action Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Direct-policy World Action Models (WAM) have demonstrated the benefits of decoupling action generation from explicit future visual prediction for efficient inference in autonomous driving and embodied control. However, they still require tens of denoising steps to achieve competitive action quality, incurring substantial latency and hindering real-time deployment. Simply reducing the number of denoising steps will collapse the nonlinear multi-step denoising trajectory into coarse updates, substantially degrading action quality. To reduce the denoising steps while enabling real-time action generation, we present an effective world action model with one-step action generation, namely OSWAM, for autonomous driving and embodied control. We argue that it is the absence of structured action priors in random noise initialization that forces direct-policy WAMs to recover coherent action sequences through iterative denoising. Hence, we construct imagination tokens to initialize the diffusion process, providing physical priors and action-conditioned representations. We further introduce privileged information distillation with future conditioning to enhance future-aware action generation. As a result, OSWAM can efficiently and effectively generate high quality actions in just one diffusion step. Our experiments demonstrate that OSWAM achieves comparable or even better results in both autonomous driving and embodied control than direct-policy WAM and Joint-WAM that require tens of steps. It obtains approximately $3\times$ speedup over direct-policy WAM baselines and supports real-time compiled inference with latency as low as 40ms on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. The project page is available at https://gwenzhang.github.io/OSWAM/

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Physical intelligence [1, 2], including autonomous driving [3] and embodied control [4], holds the promise of freeing human workers from physical tasks that are dangerous, laborious, or tedious. general-purpose physical agent should not only act from visual observations, but also anticipate the physical consequences of their actions. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, including those standard models [57] and specialized end-to-end ones [810], typically predict actions directly without explicitly modeling the future evolution of the environment. This has motivated shift toward World Action Models (WAMs) [4, 1113] for physical AI, which build on pretrained video generative models [14, 15] to jointly predict future visual states and their corresponding actions. However, WAMs follow the imagine-then-execute paradigm [12, 16] and incur prohibitive inference latency, rendering them impractical for latency-critical applications such as autonomous driving. Borrowing few-step techniques from image and video generation, some methods apply step distillation [17] to reduce this latency, but often at the expense of substantial drop in control accuracy, as illustrated in Fig. 1. To address this issue, efforts [4, 11] propose to switch from the imagine-then-execute paradigm to direct-policy WAMs. These Visual Computing Lab The Hong Kong Polytechnic University 1 / 19 Figure 1. Quantitative comparison of the Fast-WAM [4] test-time scaling with different action denoising steps on (a) the autonomous driving dataset Navsim, and (b) embodied control dataset RoboTwin. methods retain video prediction as training-time objective that shapes physically grounded representations, without synthesizing future observations at test time. This direct-policy formulation is more than 3 faster than the imagine-then-execute paradigm. Despite this speedup, efficiently generating high-quality actions remains key challenge for direct-policy WAMs. They require tens of denoising steps to achieve competitive action quality, resulting in latency that remains too high for real-time applications such as autonomous driving. This bottleneck cannot be resolved by reducing the number of denoising steps. Specifically, as shown in Fig. 2, the performance degrades as the step count decreases, dropping by 20% on NAVSIM (autonomous driving) and 40% on RoboTwin (embodied control) in the one-step setting. We attribute this to the lack of action structure in random noise: multiple denoising steps can gradually impose temporal and physical consistency, whereas one-step generation must recover coherent action sequence in single update. Existing few-step accelerations, such as step distillation [17] and trajectory rectification [18], still start from Gaussian noise and, therefore, do not supply the missing action prior. This motivates introducing structured action priors at initialization, providing an informed starting point for high-quality action generation in single denoising step. In addition, direct-policy WAMs [4, 11] remain limited in their ability to exploit future dynamics for effective control. They use consistent first-frame-only interface during training and inference, relying on video co-training to encode future dynamics into the current representation. However, compressing all future information into single first-frame representation may provide insufficient temporal context for effective future-aware control. To address this limitation, subsequent methods reintroduce future features at inference and mitigate the associated rollout cost through caching, sparse interaction [19], or compact latent representations [20]. Despite these efforts to reduce rollout cost, generating and incorporating future features at test time still incurs additional inference overhead. To address the aforementioned issues, we propose OSWAM, world action model with one-step action generation for more effective physical control. Our key observation is that previous one-step action generation methods fail mainly because the action diffusion processing is initialized from unstructured Gaussian noise. To supply the missing action structure, we learn compact set of imagination tokens from the video Diffusion Transformer (DiT) and use them as structured start points for action denoising. These tokens are far fewer than video first-frame tokens and are obtained in single forward pass, so they add negligible computation, yet they interact with visual features to accumulate physically grounded, action-relevant context. We then Visual Computing Lab The Hong Kong Polytechnic University 2 / noise the imagination tokens to an intermediate timestep and decode them with the action DiT in one step, replacing the long denoising trajectory required by random initialization. To enhance future-aware control, we train these imagination tokens with privileged-information distillation. teacher attends to visual tokens over the full future horizon, while the student imagination tokens, at test time, attend only to the first frame. By distilling the teachers privileged representations into the imagination tokens and subsequently into the action DiT, OSWAM transfers long-horizon context without reintroducing future-dependent features at inference. This design preserves the first-frame-only interface of direct-policy WAMs, while enabling high-quality action generation in single denoising step. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose OSWAM, world action model that enables high-quality one-step action generation. It learns compact imagination tokens from the video DiT as structured start points for the action DiT. These tokens are obtained in single forward pass with negligible overhead and are decoded in one denoising step. We introduce privileged-information distillation to transfer long-horizon context into the imagination tokens. teacher attends to visual tokens over the full future horizon, while the student remains first-frame-only at test time, preserving the interface of direct-policy WAMs without future-dependent features at inference. Experiments on autonomous driving and embodied control show that OSWAM achieves competitive results with multi-step WAMs while being substantially faster.

sections.title:
2.3 Effective World Action Models
The main deployment bottleneck for WAMs lies in the high computational cost of diffusion-based video and
action generators, whose test-time latency is prohibitive for onboard driving and closed-loop manipulation.
sections.content: Visual Computing Lab The Hong Kong Polytechnic University 3 / 19 Figure 3. The overall architecture of OSWAM. single Video DiT pass produces an observation-conditioned action prior with AIT and complementary scene context with SIT, providing structured initialization for one-step Action DiT denoising. Privileged-information distillation injects future-informed representations during training, while inference uses only the current observation. Drawing one-step distillation from video generation, Flash-WAM [17] compresses joint video-action diffusion to single denoising step per modality, but still synthesizes future video at inference. Fast-WAM [4] removes test-time video rollout by predicting actions from current observations only, yet retains iterative action denoising. Light-WAM [34] further replaces the generative action expert with lightweight fusion head for single-pass action prediction, but underperforms on challenging benchmarks such as RoboTwin. SimWAM [11] follows Fast-WAM to drop test-time video rollout, but its multi-step action denoising keeps inference latency well above the budget required for onboard deployment. Building on this video-rollout-free direct-policy formulation, OSWAM addresses the remaining action-generation bottleneck through one-step action denoising.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: We present OSWAM, direct-policy world action model that enables high-quality one-step action generation for autonomous driving and embodied control. The preliminary concepts associated with our method are provided in Sec. 3.1. In the following sections, we first present the overall architecture of OSWAM, then describe in detail the fundamental components of OSWAM, including imagination tokens, Role-aware 3D RoPE, and privileged-information distillation.

sections.title:
3.2 Overall Architecture
An overview of OSWAM is shown in Fig. 3. As in previous works [4, 11], we consider predicting an action
chunk a1:𝐻 from the current frame 𝑓0 and an optional task instruction 𝑙, with ego-state information additionally
provided for driving tasks. We follow Fast-WAM in the world model backbone configuration and direct-policy
setting. Specifically, the Video DiT uses the Wan2.2-5B backbone [14], accompanied by its pretrained T5 text
encoder and video VAE. The Action DiT is initialized by interpolating and downsampling the pretrained Video
DiT weights. For autonomous driving, we add an ego encoder to encode the ego state and the driving command.
The task languages and ego states are both provided to all tokens through cross-attention. The full model is
organized as a Mixture-of-Transformer (MoT) architecture with shared attention between the video and action
blocks. We also follow the direct-policy protocol: video modeling is used only as a training signal, and future
video is not rolled out at inference.
sections.content: Unlike prior direct-policy methods, which use the Video DiT at inference solely to encode the first-frame visual feature for Action DiT through shared MoT attention, OSWAM additionally introduces two groups of imagination tokens into the Video DiT: Action Imagination Tokens (AIT) and Scene Imagination Tokens (SIT). As shown in Fig. 3, both AIT and SIT are initialized from noise in the Video DiT and interact with the first-frame visual features. The resulting AIT representation then replaces the unstructured Gaussian initialization of the Action DiT, providing compact, structured start point for action denoising. SIT provides additional latent slots that aggregate scene context for AIT; they are updated indirectly through privileged distillation and the auxiliary action loss on AIT. Together, AIT and SIT comprise far fewer tokens than the first-frame visual input and therefore introduce only small computational overhead during inference. To strengthen future-aware control under this first-frame-only interface, we introduce privileged-information distillation. The privileged teacher comprises Video DiT with AIT that attends to visual tokens over the full clip, while the AIT in OSWAM attends only first-frame visual context. By aligning OSWAMs intermediate imagination token features with those of the teacher, we transfer this privileged information to improve action generation, while OSWAM remains first-frame-only at inference.

3.4 Privileged-Information Distillation
Although imagination tokens provide a structured action prior, long-horizon context is only implicitly
encoded in the first-frame representation. We therefore introduce privileged-information distillation to transfer
representations learned from privileged future observations into OSWAM’s AIT, strengthening their predictive
capability without requiring future observations at inference.
sections.content: We separately train Video DiT teacher with auxiliary AIT, following the same training settings as OSWAM except for the token groups and attention masks. As shown in Fig. 4 (a), the teacher contains video tokens Visual Computing Lab The Hong Kong Polytechnic University 6 / 19 and AIT, with AIT attending to the full video clip. OSWAM additionally includes SIT, and its AIT attends to first-frame visual tokens, SIT, and other AIT, while SIT attends only to first-frame visual tokens and other SIT. During distillation, we freeze the teacher and provide it with ground-truth video latents over the full future horizon. The first-frame latents remain clean, while all future-frame latents are corrupted with noise at fixed diffusion timestep 𝜏𝑇 𝑣 before the teacher forward pass. The teachers AIT remains initialized from pure noise at 𝑡max and acquires privileged information by attending to these future video tokens. OSWAM retains its standard training procedure, using randomly sampled video timestep and the fixed AIT timestep 𝑡max. The teacher and OSWAM share the same video noise and action noise samples, respectively. We then align OSWAMs AIT features with the corresponding teacher features at set of Video DiT blocks , providing multi-depth distillation supervision. SIT is supervised indirectly through their attention connections to AIT. At inference, the teacher is discarded, preserving OSWAMs first-frame-only interface without additional computation.

sections.title:
4.1 Datasets and Evaluation Metrics
Autonomous Driving. For autonomous driving, we evaluate OSWAM on the NAVSIM [43], which provides
real-world driving data sampled at 2Hz, with eight cameras covering a 360-degree field of view and LiDAR
observations. The dataset comprises 1192 scenarios for training and 136 scenarios for testing. NAVSIM
introduces practical and reliable metrics that effectively bridge open-loop and closed-loop evaluation. Specifically,
NAVSIM evaluates model performance using the Predictive Driver Model Score (PDMS), which is calculated
based on five factors: No At-Fault Collision (NC), Drivable Area Compliance (DAC), Time-to-Collision
(TTC), Comfort (Comf.), and Ego Progress (EP). We report PDMS, which is calculated as PDMS =
NC × DAC × (5 × EP + 5 × TTC + 2 × C)/12.

sections.title:
4.2 Implementation Details
Following Fast-WAM, we initialize OSWAM from Wan2.2-5B and adopt the Action DiT with a reduced hidden
dimension of 1024. The imagination-token LoRA adapters use rank 8 and 𝛼 = 4. For NAVSIM, we follow [11]
to use a single front camera at 384 × 672 resolution and predict eight waypoints over four seconds at 2Hz. We
use the current frame and eight future frames in training. For RoboTwin, we concatenate the head and two wrist
views into a 384 × 320 image and use an action horizon of 32, with nine video frames sampled at a temporal
stride of 4. For temporal RoPE, we set 𝑠𝑎 = 1 and 𝑑𝑡 = 4 on both benchmarks, with 𝑠𝑣 = 1 for NAVSIM
and 𝑠𝑣 = 4 for RoboTwin. AIT and SIT therefore use 𝑡𝑛 = 𝑛/4, (𝑛 = 1, . . . , 8) on NAVSIM and 𝑡𝑛 = 𝑛/16,
(𝑛 = 1, . . . , 32) on RoboTwin; video latents use temporal coordinates {0, 1, 2} in training.
sections.content: We train with AdamW using learning rate of 104, weight decay of 0.01, and cosine decay with 5% linear warmup. NAVSIM training runs for 40,000 steps with global batch size of 256, while RoboTwin training runs for 29,335 steps with global batch size of 1024. For distillation, the frozen teacher uses video timestep of 200, and feature alignment is applied after Video DiT blocks [8, 16, 24, 30]. We set 𝜆dist = 10. Distillation starts after 500 steps, with its weight increasing linearly over the next 500 steps. Across both benchmarks, we set the AIT diffusion timestep to 𝑡max = 1000 and the re-noising timestep for Action DiT initialization to 𝜏𝑟 = 500 (𝜎𝑟 = 0.5). During inference, we use single Action DiT denoising step. Unless otherwise specified, all latency measurements are conducted on single NVIDIA H20 GPU and Intel Xeon Max 9468 CPU.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: In this paper, we presented OSWAM, an efficient world-action model for one-step action generation. To address the reliance of direct-policy WAMs on iterative action denoising, we introduced Action Imagination Tokens to learn structured initialization, supported by Scene Imagination Tokens that aggregate complementary scene context. We further developed privileged-information distillation to transfer full future context into the Action Imagination Tokens. Together, these designs enable action generation with single Video DiT pass and one Action DiT denoising step. Experiments on NAVSIM and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrated the competitive planning and manipulation performance of OSWAM and its substantial latency reductions over direct-policy baselines. OSWAM offers practical approach to efficient world-action modeling for latency-critical control. Limitations. Our study is focused on learning action DiT structured initialization. Although SIT and privileged-information distillation support this objective, their potential to directly enhance the Action DiT remains unexplored. Extending scene-context conditioning and privileged supervision to the action expert is promising direction for future work.

sections.content: A.1 More Implementation Details nuScene. We also evaluate OSWAM on the nuScenes [47] dataset for autonomous driving. nuScenes comprises 1,000 real-world driving scenes, with keyframes annotated at 2 Hz. The scene images are captured by 6 cameras covering 360 degree FOV horizontally. The dataset is split into 700 scenes for training, 150 for validation, and 150 for testing. Following previous works [41, 48], 𝐿2 Displacement Error (DE) and Collision Rate (CR) are adopted to comprehensively evaluate the planning performance. For nuScenes, we use single front camera at 384 672 resolution. Each training sample contains the current frame and eight future frames sampled at 2Hz. We use eight action steps to match the four-second video horizon, with supervision and evaluation limited to the first three seconds. Each action is represented as (𝑥, 𝑦, 𝜃) in the current LiDAR coordinate frame, with padded and unsupervised positions excluded from the action loss. For Role-aware 3D RoPE, we set 𝑠𝑎 = 𝑠𝑣 = 1 and 𝑑𝑡 = 4, giving AIT and SIT temporal coordinates 𝑡𝑛 = 𝑛/4 for (𝑛 = 1, . . . , 8). Video latents use temporal coordinates {0, 1, 2} during training. We train for 10,000 steps with global batch size of 128 using AdamW, learning rate of 104, weight decay of 0.01, and cosine decay with 5% linear warmup. For distillation, the frozen teacher uses video timestep of 200, and feature alignment is applied after Video DiT blocks [8, 16, 24, 30]. We set 𝜆dist = 10. Distillation starts after 500 steps, with its weight increased linearly over the next 500 steps. We set the AIT diffusion timestep to 𝑡max = 1000 and the re-noising timestep for Action DiT initialization to 𝜏𝑟 = 500 (𝜎𝑟 = 0.5). A.2 More Results Navsim v2. EPDMS incorporates Driving Direction Compliance (DDC), Traffic Light Compliance (TLC), Lane Keeping (LK), and Extended Comfort (EC), while extending the original comfort metric to History Comfort (HC). These results further demonstrate the effectiveness of OSWAM under more comprehensive evaluation criteria encompassing safety, traffic-rule compliance, and driving comfort. nuScene. Table A.2 reports open-loop planning performance on nuScenes. Without auxiliary supervision, OSWAM achieves an average 0.41 L2 error, matching PWM, while reducing the average collision rate from 0.04% to 0.03%. It also achieves the lowest L2 errors at 1 and 2 seconds and the lowest collision rates across all evaluated horizons. These results demonstrate that OSWAM not only accelerates action generation but also delivers strong open-loop planning performance, matching the best average L2 error while achieving the lowest average collision rate. RoboTwin Per-task Success Rates. Table B.5 reports per-task success rates across 50 manipulation tasks on RoboTwin 2.0. OSWAM matches or exceeds Light-WAM on 49 tasks under the clean setting and 46 tasks under the randomized setting. OSWAM also matches or exceeds Fast-WAM on 22 tasks under the clean setting and 15 tasks under the randomized setting. Notably, OSWAM achieves substantial gains over Fast-WAM on Open Microwave under both settings, as well as on Move Stapler Pad, Hanging Mug, and Move Can Pot under the randomized setting. Together with the 2.80 inference speedup over Fast-WAM, these findings show that OSWAM maintains competitive task-level performance while substantially reducing inference latency. One-Step Action Generation. Tables A.3 and A.4 compare OSWAM with direct policy baselines with one-step denoising setting. On NAVSIM, OSWAM achieves PDMS of 90.3, outperforming the reported one-step results of SimWAM, Metis, and DriveVA by 21.4, 3.3, and 77.1 points, respectively. On RoboTwin 2.0, OSWAM improves the average success rate from 56.59% to 90.00% over our one-step Fast-WAM baseline, with consistent gains under both Clean and Randomized settings. These results demonstrate that OSWAM enables effective one-step action generation across both autonomous driving and embodied control.

SimWAM struggles to produce smooth trajectories, particularly when turning or navigating complex interactions with surrounding agents, leading to drivable-area violations and at-fault collisions. In contrast, OSWAM handles these challenging examples with single action denoising step, producing smoother trajectories while satisfying both no-at-fault collision and drivable-area compliance criteria. Together with the real-time inference speed reported in Table 3, these results highlight the potential of OSWAM for practical deployment in autonomous driving.
